raw_response:
I'm 70 years old now, and I've been working these fields for 56 years — since I was 14. Me and my wife, we're the only ones left at home. Our children are in Shijiazhuang with their own families. I only went to primary school, so I don't know all those fancy words the extension people use, but I know peanut. I've grown it on this same 4 mu my whole life, and I know what works here.

I always plant around the beginning of May, when the soil is warm enough. Plant too early and the seeds rot in cold ground — I learned that the hard way when I was a young man. I save most of my seed from last year, shelling the pods and keeping the big kernels, but I buy a little new seed from the county store to mix in so the plants stay strong and don't get weak from saving too long.

For fertilizer, I buy three bags of compound fertilizer from the co-op for the whole field — about half a bag per mu. I spread it before planting and work it into the soil with the rotary tiller. My neighbor Old Zhang told me years ago to put down some gypsum when the yellow flowers come out — he said it helps the pods grow full and not hollow. I didn't believe him at first, but I tried it and now I do it every year. It costs a bit more, but the peanuts are bigger.

I irrigate twice from my well — once when the flowers open, and once when the pods are filling. Pumping costs electricity money, so I don't water more than I have to, but those two times are important. If it rains well in summer, maybe I skip one, but you can't count on rain anymore.

I spray herbicide once after planting to keep the weeds down. If I see aphids or other insects when I walk the field, I spray for them too, but I don't spray unless I see them. My eyes aren't what they used to be, so I walk slowly and look careful.

For labor, me and my wife do almost everything ourselves — planting, weeding, spraying, gathering. But digging peanut at 70 is tough on my back and knees. I hire two local people for two days at harvest to help pull and pile the plants. Costs 120 yuan per person per day, but I can't do it alone anymore.

I expect about 250 kg per mu of pods if the weather is normal. Last year I got 240, the year before 260. That's enough for us to eat, keep seed for next year, and sell a little for cash. I don't need to get rich — I just need enough to live and not lose money on inputs.
